title: A hundred moons
hookLine: if a hundred moons rose and a thousand suns, without the Guru it would still be dark (Asa di Var M2, ang 463)

lines: SOMEONE IN THE MIDDLE, STILL LOST.
cards: A stadium at night, every floodlight on. Every seat, every sign, every blade of grass lit up. And in the middle of all that light sits someone who still doesn't know where they're going, or why.
They can read every word on the scoreboard, and none of it tells them which way to turn. A life can look like that: full of light, screens and options, and somehow still dark inside.
Guru Angad has a salok for exactly that.

teach.b: Right after Guru Nanak's opening salok of thanks comes a second one, by Guru Angad, the second Guru.

teach.h: A HUNDRED MOONS, A THOUSAND SUNS.
teach.b: In paraphrase: if a hundred moons were to rise, and a thousand suns came up, even with all that light, without the Guru there would be pitch darkness. Chand is moon. Sooraj is sun.
Chaanan is light, the ordinary Punjabi word for brightness, daylight, a lamp's glow.
And ghor andhaar is deep, pitch-black darkness. Notice the size of the picture. One moon is enough to walk home by; one sun lights a whole world.
Guru Angad multiplies them, a hundred and a thousand, as if to say: pile up all the outer light you like. It doesn't reach the place he means.
That place is inside: the light that tells you who you are, what matters, which way to turn.

In Sikh teaching that light comes through the Guru, the Word that teaches from within, carried by the Gurus and now by the Guru Granth Sahib. Without it, a person can be surrounded by brightness and still stumble.

Set it beside yesterday's salok. Guru Nanak gave thanks for a Guru who turns humans into angels; Guru Angad explains why the thanks runs so deep: everything else, however bright, still leaves us in the dark.
And this is a student's voice. Guru Angad was Guru Nanak's disciple before he became Guru. Here, in his own salok, he says what his teacher meant to him.

how: Asa di Var's second salok, by Guru Angad, is sung each morning in gurdwaras: a hundred moons and a thousand suns would still leave darkness without the Guru.

o: a lamp lit only for prayer
the full moon rising at night

games.q: a hundred moons — tap the pairs.

s: the hundred moons salok is by Guru Nanak
it's by Guru Angad, the second Guru, Guru Nanak's disciple.
the salok says outer light, however much, can't reach the inner dark
a hundred moons and a thousand suns, and still pitch darkness without the Guru.
the salok praises the sun and moon as the true light
it multiplies them to show that outer light isn't the light it means.

games.q: a hundred moons are up, and a thousand suns. by Guru Angad's salok, can you see the way?
o: not without the Guru: it's still pitch dark.
games.why: Guru Angad says that even with all that light, without the Guru there's ghor andhaar, pitch darkness. the light he means is within.

practice: Close your eyes and cup your hands over them, or turn off the light, and let the dark be complete. Even here something in you is awake, the breath, the simple knowing that you're here; rest in that small inner light.
If you pray, say Waheguru into the dark.

wordCard.voice: Chaanan, light or brightness: Guru Angad's salok asks what a hundred moons and a thousand suns, all that chaanan, can do, leaving pitch darkness without the Guru, the light within.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: chaanan, light or brightness; the salok asks what all that chaanan can do without the Guru.

carryVoice: Your line: the guru is the light. All the moons in the sky can't stand in for it. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Asa di Var, salok Mahala 2 before pauri 1, Guru Angad (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 463)
